data.name: Vaud
data.summary: Vaud, figures for Lausanne (cantonal coefficient 155% + communal 78.5%; cantonal income tax reduced by 5% in 2026). Dividends/income top marginal 41.5% (11.5% federal + 30% cantonal and communal ceiling, LICom art. 8). Wealth tax top marginal 0.792% (3.39 per mille x 233.5%; CHF 77,632 on CHF 10M). Children are taxed on inheritance (progressive to 3.5% cantonal, doubled by Lausanne), but the tax is halved for foreigners who never worked in Switzerland (LMSD art. 36): about 3.5% above CHF 1.3M per child. Lump-sum taxation available (CHF 445,000 a year on a CHF 1M base). Note: the '12%' initiative accepted on 27 September 2026 cuts the cantonal coefficient from the 2027 tax year.

regimes.name: Ordinary taxation (national figures = City of Zurich)
regimes.description: Ordinary residence taxation: federal income tax plus cantonal and communal income and wealth taxes. Switzerland has 26 cantonal tax systems; the national numbers here represent the City of Zurich (married couple, 3 children, no church membership). See data/subnational/CHE.json for all 26 cantons.
regimes.eligibility: Swiss tax residence: domicile with intent to stay, or a stay of 30 days with work / 90 days without work (DBG art. 3). Non-EU/EFTA nationals need a residence permit.

capital_gains.summary: No tax on capital gains from private movable assets (listed shares, bonds, funds, private company shares) for a private investor (DBG art. 16 para. 3; same in all cantons). Gains on Swiss real estate are taxed by the cantonal real estate gains tax: Holding-period tariff 30% (<1 yr) falling to 7% (24+ yrs); 14% for 10-11 years; years of owner-occupation count double.
capital_gains.exemptions_thresholds: Private movable-asset gains are fully exempt; private losses are not deductible.
capital_gains.eligibility_conditions: Applies only while the person is a private investor and not a professional securities dealer (ESTV Circular 36).
capital_gains.regional_differences: Real estate gains tax tariffs, holding-period reductions and multipliers differ by canton.
capital_gains.important_exceptions: Gains can be recharacterised as taxable income: professional securities dealing; indirect partial liquidation (sale of >=20% stake to a company that distributes old reserves within 5 years, DBG art. 20a); transposition (sale of >=5% stake to a company you control at least 50%); liquidation surpluses and share buybacks are taxed as dividends.

open_questions: Real estate rate is an approximation for a CHF 1M gain held exactly 10 years on a non-owner-occupied property; actual tax depends on holding period, gain size and commune.
capital_gains.rate_basis: Securities: statutory exemption of private capital gains. Real estate: approximate effective cantonal/communal real estate gains tax on a CHF 1,000,000 gain, held 10 full years, not owner-occupied, computed from the ESTV Steuermäppchen 2025 tariff table. Foreign real estate gains are exempt in Switzerland.
capital_gains.professional_trader: ESTV Circular 36 safe harbour (all must be met): holding period of at least 6 months; annual transaction volume at most 5x the portfolio at the start of the year; gains not needed to replace missing income (gains under 50% of net income); investments not debt-financed, or taxable investment income exceeds interest paid; derivatives used only to hedge own positions. Outside the safe harbour a facts-and-circumstances test applies; if classified as a dealer, all gains become taxable income (plus social security contributions), but losses become deductible.
capital_gains.holding_period_rules: No holding period for movable assets. For >=10% business holdings the partial taxation of gains needs 1 year (business assets only).
capital_gains.foreign_assets: Gains on foreign securities and foreign real estate are exempt; foreign real estate counts only for rate progression in income/wealth tax.

dividends.summary: Dividends are ordinary income. Cantonal and communal income tax on large incomes hits the 30% ceiling of LICom art. 8 para. 1 (the barème alone would give about 32.9% for a CHF 2M income at Lausanne multipliers), so the top combined marginal rate in Lausanne is 41.5% (federal 11.5% + 30%), church tax excluded. Only for holdings of at least 10% is the dividend partially taxed (federal 70%, cantonal 70%), giving about 29.0%. Portfolio dividends are taxed in full.
dividends.exemptions_thresholds: Partial taxation needs a stake of at least 10% of share capital: federal 70% taxable (DBG art. 20 para. 1bis), cantonal 70% taxable (StHG art. 7 para. 1, minimum 50%).
dividends.regional_differences: Communal multipliers vary within the canton; figures are for the cantonal capital.
dividends.important_exceptions: Church tax (if a member of a recognised church) adds roughly 1-3 points and is excluded here. The '12%' initiative accepted on 27 September 2026 cuts the cantonal coefficient by 12% (from 2027); at 30% ceiling income this changes nothing for the largest incomes while the ceiling binds.

dividends.rate_basis: Statutory: federal 11.5% (DBG art. 36 para. 2) + the Vaud maximum of 30% of income for cantonal plus communal income tax (LICom art. 8 para. 1, Feuille cantonale 2026). Without the ceiling the tax would be 15.5% top category (art. 47 LI) x (155% x 0.95 [5% cut, LRIPP art. 4] + 78.5% communal) = 35.0% at the margin, so the ceiling binds above about CHF 600,000 of income. Agrees with the ESTV-calculator figure (41.5%). Swiss 35% withholding tax is refunded to residents who declare the dividend.
dividends.withholding_outbound: Swiss companies withhold 35% Verrechnungssteuer on dividends; refundable to Swiss residents, reduced by treaty for non-residents (residual 0-20%).
dividends.treaty_network: About 100 income tax treaties (PwC: 99 in force at 1 December 2025). Non-recoverable treaty-rate foreign WHT is credited (flat-rate credit) against Swiss tax.
dividends.holding_company_notes: Company-level participation reduction for holdings of 10% or CHF 1M (DBG art. 69); see corporate.

wealth_tax.summary: Annual cantonal and communal net wealth tax on worldwide net assets (no federal wealth tax). In Lausanne the top combined marginal rate is 0.792% (3.39 per mille x 233.5%). Tax on CHF 10M taxable wealth: CHF 77,632; on CHF 50M: CHF 394,258 (0.79% average), before the burden cap.
wealth_tax.exemptions_thresholds: No social deductions: a couple whose net wealth is below CHF 120,000 pays no wealth tax (LI art. 58, 2026 amount; a cliff: above it the whole wealth is taxed from the first franc). Fractions below CHF 1,000 are dropped. The tariff and the CHF 60,000 / 120,000 amounts are fully adjusted to prices every year (LI art. 60). Household effects are exempt; debts are deductible.
wealth_tax.eligibility_conditions: Applies to all persons with unlimited tax liability in the canton (domicile or 30/90-day stay rules).
wealth_tax.regional_differences: Communal multipliers vary within the canton; figures are for the cantonal capital.
wealth_tax.important_exceptions: Burden caps (LICom art. 8): cantonal and communal income tax at most 30% of income, wealth tax at most 10 per mille, income plus wealth tax at most 60% of net income with the net wealth yield counted at least 1% (LA 2026 art. 7), and the wealth tax after the cap never below 3 per mille. On 27 September 2026 voters accepted the '12%' initiative, so the 2022 version of the bouclier fiscal stays (the 2024 revision was subject to a 'clause guillotine'); on 6 October 2026 the Grand Conseil majority asked the government to revive the 2024 changes (a referendum is announced). The 60% cap and the 3 per mille floor are in income_cap; the 30% income ceiling is inside the dividend rate.

components.name: Cantonal + communal net wealth tax (Lausanne, 2026)
components.notes: Combined cantonal + communal marginal rates on net wealth: the 2026 base tariff of LI art. 59 (0.97 / 1.69 / 2.42 / 3.15 / 3.39 per mille above CHF 60,000 / 95,000 / 177,000 / 355,000 / 711,000; the first band is set so the base tax at CHF 711,000 equals the CHF 1,757.35 of the ACI's 2026 summary table, the statute text printing only the 2025 first band) x (cantonal coefficient 155% + Lausanne 78.5% = 233.5%). entry_threshold 120,000 = the couple's tax-free net wealth (a cliff). Church tax excluded. Burden caps: see income_cap.

income_cap.notes: LICom art. 8 paras. 3, 3bis, 3ter and LA 2026 art. 7 (Vaud, version in force since 2022, kept by the 27 September 2026 vote): cantonal and communal income plus wealth tax at most 60% of net income, the net wealth yield counted at least 1% of net wealth, and the wealth tax after the cap never below 3 per mille of wealth (min_wealth_tax_rate; max_reduction 1 because no other limit applies). counted_income_tax_rate 0.30 = the 30% income-tax ceiling of art. 8 para. 1, the flat rate the tax file uses; the true rate at CHF 600,000 of income is 24%-27% depending on the family quotient. The wealth tax maximum of 10 per mille (art. 8 para. 1) is not modelled; it does not bind below a 7.9 per mille tariff. The 2024 revision, revived by a Grand Conseil motion of 6 October 2026, is not in force.

wealth_tax.property_tax_note: Some cantons/communes levy a separate annual real-property tax (Liegenschaftssteuer) on gross real estate value; it is not part of the wealth tax.

inheritance.summary: Vaud taxes inheritances to children, but halves the tax for foreigners who never worked in Switzerland and whose estate is wholly taxable in Vaud (LMSD art. 36). Each stirp deducts CHF 1,000,000 from 2025, falling by 1/100 per CHF 1,000 above it to zero at CHF 1.1M; the cantonal rate for the direct line is the general barème (3.43% at CHF 1.1M, 3.5% from CHF 1,302,000, applied to the whole share), Lausanne adds 100 centimes (arrêté d'imposition 2025-2029, chiffre VI), so 7% in all, 3.5% after the halving.
inheritance.exemptions_thresholds: CHF 1,000,000 deduction per stirp (child), phased out between CHF 1,000,000 and CHF 1,100,000. Gifts: exempt up to CHF 300,000 per child per calendar year.
inheritance.eligibility_conditions: Applies when the deceased/donor was domiciled in the canton (movable assets); Swiss real estate is taxed in the canton where it lies.
inheritance.regional_differences: Communes may levy up to 100% additional centimes; Lausanne levies 100%. Other communes may levy less.
inheritance.important_exceptions: LMSD art. 36: the tax on the estate of a foreigner (domiciled in Vaud, never gainfully active in Switzerland) is reduced by half, for the part wholly taxable in Vaud without a foreign share under a double tax treaty; dual nationals do not qualify. A motion (25_MOT_65) would remove the cut for lump-sum taxpayers. The brackets below already include the halving.

inheritance.spouse_note: Surviving spouse (and registered partner) is exempt from cantonal inheritance and gift tax (LMSD art. 20 let. e). Unlike descendants, who pay up to 3.5% (7% with Lausanne centimes, halved for foreign non-workers), the spouse pays nothing.
inheritance.gift_tax: Gifts to a child are exempt up to CHF 300,000 per calendar year; above that the whole gift is taxed at the same barème (halved for a foreign donor under art. 36 LMSD).
inheritance.foreign_assets: The canton of last domicile taxes worldwide movable assets; foreign real estate is not taxed. Switzerland has only a few inheritance tax treaties; gift tax is not covered by treaties.
inheritance.domicile_rules: Taxing right follows the last domicile of the deceased or the domicile of the donor. No tail after leaving Switzerland (except on Swiss real estate).

regimes.name: Lump-sum taxation (Besteuerung nach dem Aufwand / forfait fiscal)
regimes.description: Income and wealth tax are replaced by a tax on a deemed income equal to worldwide living expenses, at least the highest of: a cantonal minimum (federal: CHF 435,000 in 2026), 7x annual rent or rental value of the home, and the control calculation (ordinary tax on Swiss-source income and assets plus foreign income for which treaty relief is claimed). The ordinary tariffs are applied to that base. Not available in Zurich, Schaffhausen, Appenzell Ausserrhoden and Basel-Stadt; effectively not in Basel-Landschaft.
regimes.eligibility: Available in 2026. Cantonal minimum base CHF 415,000, which includes a 15% surcharge for the wealth tax (LI art. 15 para. 3 a); 7x the rent or rental value, increased by 10%, if higher (para. 3 b); federal minimum CHF 435,000 (DBG art. 14 para. 3 a, indexed). Both spouses must be non-Swiss, newly resident (or back after 10+ years) and not gainfully active in Switzerland.
regimes.duration_note: No time limit in law: lump-sum taxation continues for as long as the person keeps meeting the conditions of DBG art. 14 / StHG art. 6, i.e. remains a non-Swiss citizen with unlimited tax liability and takes up no gainful activity in Switzerland. It ends on naturalisation, on starting gainful work in Switzerland, or if the canton abolishes it (as Zurich, Schaffhausen, Appenzell Ausserrhoden and Basel-Stadt did); the taxpayer may also switch to ordinary taxation. The tax base is reassessed annually and the cantonal minimums are indexed.

lump_sum.notes: Estimate for a family on an expenditure base of CHF 1,000,000 (assumed 7x the rent of a family home; a prime-rent sample of CHF 9,800 a month would give CHF 823,200): federal CHF 115,000 (DBG art. 14 para. 4, no child reduction) + cantonal and communal CHF 330,000 = the 30% ceiling (LICom art. 8 para. 1) on the cantonal base of CHF 1,100,000 (7x the rent plus 10%, LI art. 15 para. 3 b; the barème at 155% x 0.95 + 78.5%, with the quotient reduction capped by art. 43 para. 3, would give about 31%). No separate wealth tax. Lausanne levies the special tax on foreigners at 0.785 of the cantonal base tax (arrêté d'imposition, chiffre V), the same coefficient as for ordinary taxpayers. Minimum base: the highest of CHF 415,000 (including 15% for the wealth tax), 7x the rent or rental value plus 10%, and the worldwide living costs (LI art. 15 para. 3); the CHF 415,000 is adjusted to prices every year (art. 60). The real base is the higher of these and a control calculation (art. 15 para. 4). The ESTV-calculator estimate used before (CHF 459,200) took a base of CHF 1.15M.

dividends.summary: Foreign dividends are not taxed separately; they are covered by the lump sum unless treaty relief (reduced foreign WHT) is claimed, in which case they enter the control calculation (modified lump sum). Swiss dividends enter the control calculation at ordinary rates.
dividends.exemptions_thresholds: No separate tax on foreign investment income within the lump sum.
dividends.regional_differences: Cantonal minimum bases and wealth surcharges differ.
dividends.important_exceptions: Claiming treaty-reduced WHT (e.g. on US, French, German, Italian, Belgian, Austrian, Canadian, Norwegian dividends under the respective treaties) requires including that income in the base and paying ordinary Swiss tax on it; otherwise the full foreign statutory WHT is suffered without credit.

income.name: Switzerland

income_tax.summary: Income tax in Switzerland is levied federally, cantonally and by municipality. For a single resident of the City of Zurich the combined 2026 marginal rate reaches about 41.0% between CHF 185,100 and CHF 793,900 (federal 13.2% plus Zurich cantonal 13% x 2.14). Employees pay AHV/IV/EO 5.3% and unemployment 1.1% (capped at CHF 148,200) plus non-occupational accident cover and pension fund; the self-employed pay about 10% AHV on net profit. Health insurance is a separate mandatory personal premium.
income_tax.self_employed_notes: Self-employed pay both halves of AHV/IV/EO: about 10.0% of net profit uncapped (sliding scale from about 5.4% at low income; minimum about CHF 530 a year); second pillar (BVG) is optional for sole proprietors, Pillar 3a up to CHF 36,288 without a pension fund. Rate comes from a secondary guide; PwC says only that the self-employed cover employer and employee shares.
income_tax.local_tax_note: Combined single-filer schedule for the City of Zurich: federal direct tax scale (marginal 0.77% to 13.2%, 11.5% above CHF 793,900) plus Zurich basic tax (marginal 2% to 13%) multiplied by the cantonal factor 0.95 plus the City of Zurich municipal factor 1.19 = 2.14. Church tax (factor 0.08-0.14) excluded. Both levels are applied to the same income, ignoring different deductions. Cantonal variation is large: municipal factors in Zurich canton range 0.71 to 1.28, and other cantons (Zug, Schwyz) are much lower while Geneva is higher; one guide estimates tax on CHF 100,000 taxable profit at about CHF 15,000-18,000 in Zug versus about CHF 28,000 in Geneva (not verified). Employee 6.4% = AHV/IV/EO 5.3 + ALV 1.1; ALV is capped at CHF 148,200 and nothing is levied above, so the cap is shown as none for the AHV. Not included: non-occupational accident premium 1-4% and pension fund (BVG) contributions.

income.residence_routes: EU/EFTA citizens have a right to work under the free movement agreement and mainly register with the canton (permit is essentially a registration). Non-EU/EFTA nationals (including US) need a work permit tied to a Swiss employer or business; annual quotas apply to third-country permits (figures not verified from an opened page). Switzerland has no digital nomad visa and non-EU remote workers cannot simply settle. Any person living 90+ days in Switzerland (30 if working) becomes tax resident.
open_questions: No dedicated nomad visa confirmed on an official SEM page.
Other cantons not modelled; only the City of Zurich.

succession.name: Switzerland
succession.summary: Children and the spouse are each guaranteed half of their intestate share, and a will cannot remove it. A foreigner domiciled in Switzerland can choose the law of one of their nationalities. Switzerland has no trust law but has recognised foreign trusts since 2007, and family foundations are allowed only for narrow purposes.
succession.reserved_share: Descendants and spouse or registered partner: half of their statutory share each; parents are no longer protected. The free portion is therefore 1/2 to 3/4 depending on the heirs (Civil Code art. 470-471, since the reform in force 1 January 2023).
succession.foreign_law_note: Federal Act on Private International Law art. 90 para. 2: a foreigner may choose by will or inheritance contract the law of one of their home states; the choice lapses if they later lose that nationality or become Swiss. Swiss courts at the last domicile stay competent and Swiss real estate is subject to Swiss jurisdiction. Not under the EU Regulation.
succession.trust_note: The Hague Trusts Convention is in force for Switzerland since 1 July 2007 (HCCH table: signed 3 April 2007, ratified 26 April 2007), so foreign trusts are recognised. Switzerland has no domestic trust law. Foundations (Civil Code art. 80 ff.) are common, but family foundations may only serve education, endowment, support of family members in need or similar purposes (art. 335), so a general family-wealth foundation is not possible.
open_questions: Cantonal tax treatment of foreign trusts was not examined.
Article numbers and the PILA wording were given from general knowledge and secondary guides; confirm at fedlex.admin.ch.

assumptions: The family is two non-Swiss spouses who have not been Swiss tax residents for 10 years and do not work in Switzerland, so lump-sum taxation is open to them (LI art. 15 paras. 1-2; DBG art. 14). Both must qualify.

Lausanne, tax year 2026: cantonal coefficient 155%, communal 78.5%, the cantonal base income tax cut by 5% (communal coefficient taken on the base tax before that cut, which does not matter where the 30% ceiling binds), no church tax. The '12%' initiative accepted on 27 September 2026 would cut the cantonal coefficient by 12% from 2027; the projection keeps the 2026 coefficient.
The 30% ceiling on cantonal plus communal income tax (LICom art. 8 para. 1) is assumed to apply to the lump sum too, as in the ESTV calculator.

The lump-sum base is shown at CHF 1,000,000 (cantonal base CHF 1,100,000 with the 10% surcharge), the representative used for every canton. The family's actual base is the highest of CHF 415,000, 7 times the rent or rental value plus 10% and the living costs; with the prime-rent sample of CHF 9,800 a month (7 x 117,600 = CHF 823,200, +10% = CHF 905,520) the lump sum would be about CHF 390,000.

The 50% reduction of the inheritance tax (LMSD art. 36) requires that the deceased never exercised gainful activity in Switzerland and that no foreign state shares the right to tax the estate; it is applied at both deaths (years 30 and 60). A motion (25_MOT_65) asks to remove it for lump-sum taxpayers. The burden cap is modelled with income_cap in the 2022 version that the 27 September 2026 vote left in force.

A Swiss family foundation (ZGB art. 335) is not offered as a path: it is taxed as a legal entity, its distributions are taxable for the beneficiaries, and it brings no advantage over holding personally.
Treaty relief on foreign dividends is assumed to be claimed only if the control calculation stays below the lump sum; the 15% withholding is then a final cost.
open_questions: Needs an engine change: the lump sum is a fixed amount per regime, but by law it is the tax on a base of at least the highest of CHF 415,000 (indexed each year), 7 times the rent plus 10% and the family's worldwide living costs (LI art. 15 para. 3; DBG art. 14 para. 3). The engine would need the base as a function of the family's spending and housing cost.

Needs an engine change: modified lump sum. Claiming treaty-reduced withholding on foreign dividends puts that income into the control calculation at the ordinary barème (LI art. 15 para. 4 f, DBG art. 14 para. 3 d); the tax is the higher of the two. The engine charges 15% on every foreign dividend and ignores it.

Needs an engine change: the '12%' initiative accepted on 27 September 2026 cuts the cantonal coefficient by 12% from 2027 (not read in the initiative text; per Berney Associes and the press), and the 2022 version of the bouclier fiscal stays unless the Grand Conseil motion of 6 October 2026 (revive the 2024 changes) is enacted, with a referendum announced. The tax file holds the 2026 rules.

The ESTV-calculator estimate used before for the lump sum (CHF 459,200) took a base of CHF 1.15M; the statute (LI art. 15 para. 3 b) adds 10% to 7 times the rent, giving CHF 445,000 on a CHF 1M rent multiple.

Whether the 30% ceiling applies to the dépense, and the 2026 amounts of the quotient cap of art. 43 para. 3 (stated for 2025: CHF 212,900 and CHF 23,600 a child), were not settled from the statute; with a full 3.3-part quotient the barème on CHF 1.1M would be about 28%, below the ceiling.
Inheritance halving (LMSD art. 36): whether the Lausanne communal surcharge is halved too (CHF 315,000 on the check) or only the cantonal part (CHF 472,500) is not confirmed.
Order of the foreign-tax credit and the 60% cap (LICom art. 8): not settled by the texts read.

paths.name: Holding the portfolio personally (ordinary taxation)
paths.regime: Ordinary taxation (national figures = City of Zurich)
paths.note: Dividends are ordinary income at the federal tariff and the Vaud barème with family quotient, capped at 30% of income for cantonal and communal tax (LICom art. 8 para. 1); a portfolio holding under 10% gets no partial taxation; gains on listed shares are tax-free for a private investor (DBG art. 16 para. 3); annual cantonal and communal wealth tax on worldwide net assets; children inherit with tax (LMSD), halved for foreigners who never worked in Switzerland (art. 36). The 60% bouclier fiscal is not modelled.

paths.name: Lump-sum taxation (imposition d'après la dépense)
paths.regime: Lump-sum taxation (Besteuerung nach dem Aufwand / forfait fiscal)
paths.note: Income and wealth tax are replaced by the ordinary barème applied to a deemed expenditure of at least the highest of CHF 415,000 (which includes 15% for the wealth tax) and 7 times the rent of the home plus 10%, or the living costs (LI art. 15, DBG art. 14). No time limit in law while both spouses stay non-Swiss and do not work in Switzerland. Foreign dividends and gains are covered; inheritance follows the ordinary Vaud rules (children taxed, tax halved by LMSD art. 36).

immigration.name: Switzerland
immigration.summary: EU/EFTA citizens have free movement under the Agreement on the Free Movement of Persons: those who do not work get a B permit if they have sufficient means and health and accident insurance. US and other citizens have no investor route; the realistic options are a discretionary cantonal permit for wealthy people (usually paired with lump-sum taxation), a retiree permit, or a quota-limited work permit. Lump-sum taxation (tax on living costs, not on income) is available to non-working foreigners in most but not all cantons.
immigration.naturalisation: Ordinary naturalisation after 10 years of residence with a C permit (at least 3 of the last 5 years before applying); cantons and communes add their own residence minimums (2 to 5 years locally), integration and language tests.
immigration.dual_citizenship_note: Swiss law does not require renouncing the previous citizenship; the applicant's home country may still withdraw its own.

routes.name: EU/EFTA free movement, non-working person (B permit)
routes.summary: EU and EFTA citizens who do not work can live in Switzerland with a five-year renewable B permit if they can support themselves and are insured.
routes.requirements: Entitlement under the Agreement on the Free Movement of Persons: sufficient financial means for the person and family, and health and accident insurance. SEM does not publish a fixed amount; cantons judge whether a Swiss citizen in the same position would need social assistance. Permit valid 5 years, renewable.
routes.physical_presence: Genuine residence in Switzerland (day count not sourced)
routes.family: Spouse and relatives in the descending and ascending line can follow under the same agreement.
routes.tax_note: Residents are taxed on worldwide income and wealth. Non-working EU/EFTA citizens may apply for lump-sum taxation in cantons that still offer it.

routes.name: Lump-sum taxation (Besteuerung nach dem Aufwand) with residence permit
routes.summary: Foreigners who move to Switzerland and do not work there can be taxed on their living costs instead of their worldwide income and wealth. It is a tax status that sits on top of a residence permit, not a permit itself.
routes.requirements: Federal rules (DBG art. 14, StHG art. 6): not a Swiss citizen, first Swiss residence or return after at least 10 years abroad, no gainful activity in Switzerland. Taxable base is the highest of: the federal minimum (CHF 435,000 for the 2026 direct federal tax), 7 times the annual rent or rental value (3 times pension price for hotel residents), or the household's actual living costs; a control calculation on Swiss-source income applies. Cantons set their own minimums, some higher; several cantons have abolished the regime (cantonal decisions, e.g. Zurich, Basel-Stadt, Basel-Landschaft, Schaffhausen, Appenzell Ausserrhoden). A residence permit comes first: EU/EFTA citizens through free movement, others through the discretionary permit below.
routes.physical_presence: Swiss domicile required; no fixed day count in the federal rules (cantons may add)
routes.tax_note: Lump-sum tax replaces ordinary income and wealth tax; Swiss-source income taxed normally. Federal base CHF 435,000 for 2026; cantonal bases differ (Geneva cantonal base CHF 406,651 indexed in 2021, so it is not directly comparable).

routes.name: Non-EU permit in the important public (fiscal) interest
routes.summary: Wealthy non-EU citizens without a job can sometimes get a discretionary cantonal residence permit because their tax payments are in the canton's interest. There is no fixed investment or income threshold.
routes.requirements: Discretionary permit under the Foreign Nationals and Integration Act (AIG) art. 30 para. 1 let. b, granted by the canton and approved by SEM. In practice tied to lump-sum taxation or a high tax contribution; cantons set their own expected tax amount. Not re-verified against the statute text in this session.

routes.name: Non-EU retiree permit (age 55+)
routes.summary: Retired non-EU citizens aged 55 or over can apply for a permit if they have close ties to Switzerland and enough money not to need social assistance.
routes.requirements: AIG art. 28 and the Ordinance on Admission (VZAE art. 25): minimum age 55, no gainful activity, special personal ties to Switzerland (e.g. earlier long residence, family), sufficient funds, health insurance. Cantonal and SEM approval. Statute references from earlier research, not re-verified against the text this session.

routes.name: Work permits (summary)
routes.summary: EU/EFTA citizens can take a job freely with an employment contract of at least 365 days (B permit, five years). Non-EU citizens need an employer, a permit under national quotas, and must be highly qualified.
routes.requirements: EU/EFTA: B permit on showing a contract of 365 days or more or an open-ended contract; valid 5 years, renewable. Non-EU/EFTA: AIG art. 18-21, national annual quotas, priority for Swiss and EU/EFTA workers, higher-qualified specialists only. Switzerland has no digital nomad visa.
